title: Jury selection to begin in federal hate crimes trial over Buffalo supermarket shooting | CNN
text:
Source: AP

Jury selection began Tuesday in the federal hate crime trial of a man who admitted tokilling 10 Black peoplein a massacre at a New York supermarket in 2022, a case that could lead to a rare death sentence.

Payton Gendron is alreadyspending life in prisonafter pleading guilty to state murder charges and tearfully renouncing his White supremacist views. He now faces atrial in federal courtarising from the same mass shooting. The stakes are high: If convicted, the 23-year-old could face the death penalty.

The attack at the Tops Friendly Market in Buffalo is believed to be the deadliest hate-motivated shooting targeting Black people in the US by a lone gunmanin the past century.

Gendron has pleaded not guilty to dozens of hate crime and gun charges, though his defense lawyers do not dispute his guilt. They even predicted a conviction when speaking to prospective jurors Tuesday.

If Gendron is convicted, his lawyers will try to persuade jurors to spare him from execution. Life imprisonment is typically the alternative.

“At trial, we will offer mitigating evidence about Payton that the jury needs to consider in making its decision,” his lawyers said in a statement. “Nothing we say or do is intended to be disrespectful or insensitive to the victims, the survivors, or their loved ones.”

Gendron spoke to his lawyers and took notes while attorneys and US District Judge Lawrence Vilardo interviewed people. A recurring question from the defense team: If you were king of an island, would you have a death penalty?

One person said she didn’t want to be on the jury partly because of the stress of watching a video Gendron livestreamed during the shooting.

Another said other countries might respond to such an attack by “stoning” the offender. He said he could fairly weigh the aggravating and mitigating factors if the trial reaches a death penalty phase.

A teacher was dismissed after saying that White nationalism, antisemitism and mass shootings are a “cancer popping up” and that a “life for a life would be a just result” for extreme crimes.

Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told The Associated Press that Gendron’s lawyers will try to reveal at trial “almost every aspect of his life before he committed his crime and even after he committed his crime” to try to keep him off death row.

On May 14, 2022, Gendron, then 18, drove over 200 miles from Conklin, a predominantly White, rural town, to Buffalo. He fired around 60 shots from a semiautomatic rifle at supermarket employees and shoppers. Video later revealed Gendron apologized to a White store worker after shooting him in the leg.

Investigators also found past social media posts and other writings by Gendron dedicated to planning an attack to frighten people who were non-white and non-Christian into leaving the US. He promoted a baseless“great replacement theory”that people of color will replace White people through higher birth rates and immigration.

The victimskilled were all Black and between the ages of 32 and 86. They were Celestine Chaney, Geraldine Talley, Katherine Massey, Pearl Young, Andre Mackneil, church deacon Heyward Patterson, Ruth Whitfield, Roberta Drury, Margus Morrison andAaron Salter, a retired police officer who was working as a security guard.

The Justice Department, under President Joe Biden, decided in 2024 to seek the death penalty. The government later rejected a proposal from Gendron to plead guilty in exchange for a life sentence.

Chaney’s son, Wayne Jones Sr., said thinking about her absence each day is a reason he doesn’t want to see a death penalty.

“I really think that he should just sit and have to think about it year after year after year and just be miserable,” said Jones. “When I was younger, I probably was more prone to say, ‘kill him.’ But, at this point, I mean, he’s got, what, another 20, 30 years of appeals?”

Black people have comprised the “No. 1 numerical target” annually since the FBI began collecting data in 1991, said hate crime analyst Brian Levin of the California Association of Human Relations Organizations.

According to FBI data released in August, law enforcement agencies reported over 2,800 anti-Black hate crime incidents in 2025, nearly three times the number targeting Latinos. The FBI also reported a 7% decline in hate crime incidents from 2024 to 2025.

The Buffalo shooting and the 2015 Charleston, South Carolina, church shooting, in which a White gunman killed nine Black churchgoers, show how online radicalization also made them matters of terrorism.

Buffalo Common Council member Zeneta Everhart, whose son, Zaire Goodman, survived the shooting but still has shrapnel in his body, said hate crime enhancements might be the only deterrent.

“This is domestic terrorism,” Everhart said. “It is important we go after the death penalty in this case. But if he doesn’t end up getting it, I know that justice will be served.”

Garnell Whitfield lost his 86-year-old mother, Ruth, in the shooting. He had no opinion on whether Gendron should be executed but said he hoped the trial would reveal the “radicalization, social media and societal ills” that lead people to hate-based violence.

“Those are the things that I care about,” he said.
